facts: Kirkgate Market is one of the largest indoor markets in Europe.
Marks & Spencer began as a single stall here in 1884.
Leeds station is one of the busiest outside London, a major hub for the North of England.
The Royal Armouries houses the National Collection of Arms and Armour, relocated from the Tower of London.
The museum sits on the waterfront at Leeds Dock.
Leeds was a major centre of the wool and clothing trade during the Industrial Revolution.
Meadowhall is one of the largest shopping centres in the UK, built on the site of a former steelworks.
Sheffield's Winter Garden, in the city centre, is one of the largest urban glasshouses in Europe.
Sheffield is historically famous worldwide for its steel and cutlery production.
York Minster is one of the largest cathedrals of its kind in Northern Europe.
Its Great East Window is the largest medieval stained glass window in the world.
York station, opened in 1877, was once the largest railway station in the world.
The museum holds the national collection of British railway history, including a Japanese bullet train.
It displays the Flying Scotsman and Mallard, the world's fastest steam locomotive.
York was a major railway town, home to the headquarters of the North Eastern Railway.
Saltaire is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, a model industrial village built by Sir Titus Salt in the 1850s.
Salts Mill was once the largest industrial building in the world at the time of its construction.
The mill now houses galleries including a large collection of works by artist David Hockney.
Ribblehead Viaduct has 24 arches and stands over 30 metres tall, on the Settle-Carlisle Line.
It took around 1,000 navvies several years to build, completed in 1875.
The line here crosses some of the most dramatic and remote scenery on the English rail network.
Settle is the southern gateway to one of Britain's most scenic railway lines, opened in 1876.
The line was built partly as a Midland Railway show of strength against rival companies.
Settle sits within the Yorkshire Dales National Park.
Ilkley Moor inspired the unofficial Yorkshire anthem 'On Ilkla Moor Baht 'at'.
The moor holds numerous prehistoric carved rocks, including the Cow and Calf formation.
Ilkley developed as a spa town in Victorian times, exploiting its moorland spring water.
Beverley Minster is one of the largest parish churches in England, comparable in scale to many cathedrals.
The town's medieval North Bar is one of the few surviving fortified gateways of its kind still spanning a public road.
Beverley sits in the East Riding of Yorkshire, close to Hull.
Bridlington's Old Town retains timber-framed buildings dating back centuries.
The town's harbour has been a fishing and trading port since medieval times.
Bridlington is a popular traditional seaside resort on the Yorkshire coast.
Filey Brigg is a rocky headland stretching almost a mile out into the North Sea.
Filey developed as a quieter alternative to nearby Scarbrough and Bridlington as a Victorian resort.
The town's wide sandy beach stretches for several miles.

landmark: Kinder Scout & the Pennine Way, Edale
facts: Edale is the official starting point of the Pennine Way, England's oldest long-distance National Trail.
Kinder Scout, nearby, was the site of the 1932 Mass Trespass, a landmark protest for public access to open land.
Edale sits in the Hope Valley, within the Peak District's Dark Peak area.
A grave in Hathersage churchyard is traditionally said to belong to Little John, companion of Robin Hood.
The village inspired 'Morton' in Charlotte Bronte's novel Jane Eyre.
Hathersage has an outdoor heated swimming pool dating from the 1930s.
Padley Gorge is a wooded valley known for its ancient oak woodland, a rarity in the Peak District.
Grindleford station's cafe is a popular stop for Peak District walkers.
The village sits within the Hope Valley, on the line between Sheffield and Manchester.

landmark: Dore & Totley, gateway to the Peak
facts: Dore & Totley marks the western edge of Sheffield, right at the boundary of the Peak District.
The area was historically the site of a significant Anglo-Saxon meeting between Wessex and Northumbria.
The station serves affluent residential suburbs of southwest Sheffield.
Elsecar preserves one of the best examples of an integrated ironworks and colliery site in Britain.
Its Newcomen engine, still on its original site, is the only one of its kind left in the world.
Elsecar was developed by the Earls Fitzwilliam as a planned industrial village.
Conisbrough Castle's unusual cylindrical keep, built around 1180, is one of the best-preserved in England.
It featured prominently in Sir Walter Scott's novel Ivanhoe.
Conisbrough sits between Doncaster and Sheffield on the River Don.
Doncaster Racecourse hosts the St Leger Stakes, the oldest of England's five Classic horse races, first run in 1776.
Doncaster was a major railway town, home to the 'Plant Works' that built the Flying Scotsman locomotive.
The town's name derives from a Roman fort, Danum.
Worksop is a gateway town to Sherwood Forest, legendary home of Robin Hood.
The Major Oak, in Sherwood Forest, is thought to be over 800 years old.
Worksop is nicknamed 'Gateway to the Dukeries' for the grand estates that once surrounded it.
The Hepworth Wakefield gallery is named after sculptor Barbara Hepworth, born in the city in 1903.
The gallery's angular concrete design opened in 2011 on the banks of the River Calder.
Wakefield was historically an important market and wool trading centre.
Barnsley Market has traded since medieval times and remains one of the largest in Yorkshire.
The town was historically a major centre of coal mining in South Yorkshire.
Barnsley is nicknamed the 'Chic Barnsley' after a local council campaign of the 2010s.
The Piece Hall, built in 1779, is a unique surviving cloth trading hall, once used by handloom weavers to sell pieces of cloth.
It has been restored as a public square with shops, galleries and events space.
Halifax is also home to Eureka!, a major children's science museum.

landmark: Hebden Bridge & the Pennine mill town revival
facts: Hebden Bridge's steep hillsides are lined with distinctive 'top and bottom' terraced houses, stacked to fit the slope.
The town transformed from a declining mill town into a noted centre for independent shops and the arts from the 1970s onward.
Hebden Bridge sits in the Calder Valley, on the Pennine Way.
Skipton Castle is one of the most complete medieval castles in England, having survived Civil War slighting largely intact.
Skipton is known as the 'Gateway to the Dales' for its position at the edge of the Yorkshire Dales National Park.
The town holds one of the largest street markets in North Yorkshire, dating back over 700 years.
Harrogate grew into a fashionable spa town around its sulphur wells, promoted from the 17th century onward.
The Royal Pump Room Museum sits over the most famous of the town's mineral springs.
Harrogate's Betty's Tea Room is one of the most famous traditional tea rooms in England.
Knaresborough's railway viaduct, built in 1851, is one of the most photographed in Yorkshire, spanning the River Nidd gorge.
The town's castle ruins overlook the river from a high rocky outcrop.
Mother Shipton's Cave, nearby, is linked to England's most famous historic prophetess.

landmark: Bradford's National Science and Media Museum
facts: The museum holds the first ever photographic negative, created by pioneer William Henry Fox Talbot.
Bradford was designated the UK's first UNESCO City of Film in 2009.
Bradford grew explosively during the 19th century as the world's leading wool-processing centre.
Bradford City Park features the largest man-made urban water feature in the UK.
Bradford Cathedral has origins dating back over 700 years, though much of its current form is Victorian.
The city has one of the youngest average populations of any major UK city.

landmark: Dent, the highest mainline village station
facts: Dent station is the highest mainline railway station in England, at 350 metres above sea level.
The village of Dent itself lies some way from the station, down in the valley.
The Settle-Carlisle Line through here is renowned as one of the most scenic routes in England.
Garsdale sits at a high, remote point on the Settle-Carlisle Line, historically home to a water tank for steam locomotives.
The surrounding fells are among the most sparsely populated areas of the Yorkshire Dales.
Garsdale was once a junction with a branch line to Hawes, now closed.
Horton-in-Ribblesdale is the traditional starting point for the Yorkshire Three Peaks Challenge.
Walkers aim to summit Pen-y-ghent, Whernside and Ingleborough within 12 hours.
The village sits directly on the Settle-Carlisle Line.
Kirkby Stephen sits in the upper Eden Valley, between the Yorkshire Dales and the Lake District.
The town's parish church is known locally as the 'Cathedral of the Dales'.
It is a stop on the scenic Settle-Carlisle Line.
Appleby hosts the largest traditional Gypsy and Traveller horse fair in Europe, held each June.
The town's castle has origins dating back to Norman times.
Appleby sits on the River Eden in Cumbria.
The Deep is one of the most architecturally striking aquariums in Europe, built where the River Hull meets the Humber.
Hull was UK City of Culture in 2017.
The city's Old Town retains a maze of historic streets and courts near the marina.
The Humber Bridge was the longest single-span suspension bridge in the world when it opened in 1981.
Hessle sits on the north bank of the Humber Estuary, close to the bridge's northern tower.
The bridge links the East Riding of Yorkshire to North Lincolnshire.

landmark: Goole & the Aire and Calder Navigation
facts: Goole developed as a planned inland port in the 1820s, linking canal and sea traffic.
The town is nicknamed 'Yorkshire's Only Port' despite being around 50 miles from the open sea.
Goole's distinctive water tower is a well-known local landmark.
Selby Abbey was founded in 1069 and is one of the few English abbey churches to have survived the Dissolution largely intact.
Selby was briefly home to a large coalfield developed in the 20th century, now closed.
The town sits on the River Ouse between York and Goole.
Pontefract Castle was the site of Richard II's imprisonment and death in 1400.
The town is famous for Pontefract cakes, a traditional liquorice sweet made locally for centuries.
Pontefract has three railway stations, unusually for a town of its size.
Sculptor Henry Moore was born in Castleford in 1898.
The town has a long history of glassmaking, pottery and coal mining.
Castleford sits at the confluence of the Rivers Aire and Calder.

landmark: Denby Dale & the giant pie tradition
facts: Denby Dale is famous for baking enormous commemorative pies for major national events since 1788.
The village's railway viaduct is one of the largest in West Yorkshire.
Denby Dale sits in the Pennine foothills near Huddersfield.
Penistone Viaduct, now part of the Trans Pennine Trail, was once one of the longest in South Yorkshire.
The town sits high in the Pennine foothills between Sheffield and Huddersfield.
Penistone holds a long-running agricultural show each September.
Gainsborough Old Hall is one of the best-preserved medieval manor houses in England, dating from the 1460s.
The town sits on the River Trent in Lincolnshire.
Gainsborough was an inland port historically important for trade along the Trent.
Brigg Fair, an ancient August fair, inspired composer Frederick Delius's orchestral rhapsody of the same name.
The town sits on the River Ancholme in North Lincolnshire.
Brigg's market charter dates back to the 13th century.
Doncaster's Mansion House is one of only three remaining civic mansion houses in England, alongside London and York.
The building has hosted mayors and civic events since the 1740s.
Doncaster's railway heritage includes the 'Plant Works' where the Flying Scotsman was built.
Morley's grand Victorian Town Hall reflects the wealth the town gained from woollen textile manufacturing.
The town was the birthplace of Herbert Asquith, British Prime Minister from 1908 to 1916.
Morley sits between Leeds and Wakefield.
Batley pioneered 'shoddy', a process of recycling old woollen rags into new cloth, from the early 19th century.
The town sits within West Yorkshire's 'Heavy Woollen District'.
Batley Variety Club was once a major entertainment venue hosting international stars in the 1960s and 70s.
Dewsbury Minster has origins tracing back to Anglo-Saxon Christian missionary work in the 7th century.
The town is another key centre of the historic 'shoddy' woollen recycling trade.
Dewsbury sits on the River Calder in West Yorkshire.
Bempton Cliffs holds England's largest mainland colony of breeding seabirds, including puffins and gannets.
The chalk cliffs rise up to 100 metres above the North Sea.
Bempton station serves the small village a short walk from the reserve.
Two girls from Cottingley took famous photographs in 1917 claiming to show real fairies, later revealed as a hoax.
The photographs famously convinced Sherlock Holmes creator Sir Arthur Conan Doyle of their authenticity.
Cottingley sits between Bingley and Shipley in West Yorkshire.
